newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-API data show refiners slow to switch slates.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-API data show refiners slow to switch slates.

text.p: Latest weekly inventory figures from the American Petroleum Institute (API) suggest that the downstream oil industry is having trouble responding to a sharp switch in demand, analysts said Tuesday.

The report showed that, as winter approaches, distillates stocks (mainly heating oil) were up by only around 300,000 barrels last week and actually fell in the key eastern district (PADD1) to stand almost 19 million barrels below last year's level at just above 38 million barrels.
At the same time, gasoline, which traditionally sees waning demand after the early September Labor Day holiday, saw a three million-barrel rise in stocks, rising output and rising imports.

"What is puzzling to me is, given the picture we are discussing (of a heating oil shortage and a gasoline surplus), you would think that refiners would be shifting production towards the middle of the barrel (to make more distillates)," said Cyrus Tahmassebi, an economist and president of Energy Trends Inc. in Washington D.C.
But refinery runs rose again last week, API reported, to 95.5 percent of capacity, up a half percentage point.
"It doesn't make a lot of sense. The economics clearly are better on the heating oil end of the barrel," said John Saucer, an oil industry analyst at Smith Barney in Houston.

Possible contributory factors for the refinery industry's slowness to react to market conditions is that over the past two years while gearing up for increased gasoline production they lost some of the flexibility. Also, delayed maintenance may have inhibited their ability to respond to market conditions, Saucer said.
And refiners, with their huge fixed costs, do not have many options to cut back on gasoline, their main product.

"There is a limit to how much you can do when generally 50 percent of how much you produce is going to be gasoline," said Marianne Kah, general manager of market analysis at Conoco, a unit of Dupont Co.
The distillate production usually is around 25 percent and for most refineries the output swing possibility is between five and 10 percent.

The U.S. market has the added problem of providing a market for the surplus gasoline produced in Europe. A firm distillate market there also has increased gasoline production and prices in the U.S. have looked relatively better.
That was reflected in the figures where imports of gasoline last week again jumped, rising by 166,000 barrels to 507,000 barrels.
The situation is expected to get worse before it gets better because of the slow response times of the refineries.

"You can't just switch your slate lickety-split," said a refinery engineer at Phillips Petroleum Co in Oklahoma. "We buy crude one or two months in advance and some others up to six months in advance. You usually would assume the diesel/heating oil season wouldn't start until October and there's not a lot that people can do when you get it wrong."
"It is clear that refiners are going to have to work on getting yields shifted and/or cut gasoline production," said Saucere of Smith Barney.

As for the immediate market reaction to the latest report, the bullish distillate figures and a drop of more than 2.5 million barrels in crude stocks when the volatile western region (PADD5) is excluded, was expected to overshadow the bearish gasoline story.
In after hours trading Tuesday November NYMEX crude was at $24.12/15 a barrel, up from $24.07 at the close when it gained 70 cents.
